This bill strengthens how the social media minimum age framework is enforced.
It expands the eSafety Commissioner's powers to demand documents and information from anyone relevant to compliance checks.
Civil penalties for breaking minimum age rules would double to 60,000 penalty units, worth about $99 million for a body corporate.
Expands the eSafety Commissioner's information-gathering powers to compel production of documents from any person.
Doubles the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 2, Part 4A from 30,000 to 60,000 penalty units.
Increases the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 4, Part 4A from 500 to 1,000 penalty units.
Providers of age-restricted social media platforms and the eSafety Commissioner are affected.

Tony Pasin I feel a little like an imposter talking on this bill. Many of my colleagues who know me know that I'm probably best described as a Luddite. Even as a Luddite, in this role one has to be across the role of online presences. In fact, I am wanted, recently, to describe myself to colleagues, members of the party and constituents otherwise as a 'content creator'. I've got to tell you, Mr Deputy Speaker, when I entered the parliament in 2013, if someone told me it was a condition of this role that I would have to become a digital content creator, I would have stayed in the law and transitioned to the farm. I wouldn't have sought preselection. I wouldn't have worked very hard to obtain that preselection and then worked very hard during the election of 2013 and subsequent elections since then. But the truth is that, in the modern age, if you want to share and communicate with your constituency, or if you're in business and you want to share and communicate with customers, if you're not on a digital platform then you're missing out. And young people have gained aptitude towards digital acumen faster than any other cohort in the country. I've got a 16-year-old and a 10-year-old, and their acumen around digital platforms and these things is just a sight to behold. I'm not one of those people who come in here and say that everything about online experiences is wrong. I don't conform to that view. Like everything, there need to be appropriate safeguards; there need to be appropriate barriers. That is what we're seeking to achieve here, and I of course support my colleague the member for Lindsay's amendment. But it is important that we understand that, as positive as experiences can be in the digital online environment, there are also substantial risks. Like others, I've read of very tragic circumstances. I've had constituents, parents, come to me concerned about the way algorithms are seeking to lock young people in. Argued the change would restore intergenerational equity and redirect an estimated $3 billion in savings to additional aged-care beds, packages, shorter waits and improved care.

Presented the Selection of Bills Committee's seventh report and moved its adoption; the report recommended immediate referral of four bills concerning defence, health insurance and tax reform to Senate committees with reporting dates from 13 August to 7 October 2026, while an amendment proposed referring a workplace relations bill by 10 August.
This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed, replacing the current discount system.
The package would introduce a tax floor on gains and update the method for calculating taxable profit to reflect inflation.
The new rules would start on 1 July 2027 and would apply to future gains on assets bought before that date, with exceptions for some housing and small businesses.
Replace the 50% capital gains discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with an indexation system for the cost base.
Create a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.
Apply the new rules to gains from 1 July 2027, including those on assets bought before that date, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Individuals, trusts, partnerships, and some income support recipients who make capital gains.

Admittedly, the workers are getting less bang for their buck, but tax reforms and calls for a three-day week just mount and small business is doing it so very tough. What I fear is that those opposite don't understand or appreciate the hardships of small business because in many cases they have not run one. They've run picket lines out in front of them and they've run them into the ground, but they haven't actually run a small business to save themselves, and they don't understand and appreciate the complexities facing the operators of those many, many small businesses. I ran one for nearly a decade, with a couple of others, and it's tough. Often you take home less pay yourself than you are in fact paying your employees, your workers. As to workers, yes, we saw the independent commission this week give a wage rise to Australia's lowest paid workers—bearing in mind Australia has one of the highest minimum wages anywhere. Monique Ryan While we're making generational changes to Australia's capital gains tax system, we need to ensure that wholesale reforms don't come at the expense of clear modernisations. The thresholds for small businesses claiming capital gains tax exemptions is such an area of clear modernisation. The existing CGT small-business concession regime, the SBC regime, provides a sliding scale of concessional tax treatment to business owners when they sell their businesses. That regime is preserved by this budget. Under the current Income Tax Act 1997, in order to qualify for the regime, small businesses must have either an aggregated turnover of less than $2 million or combined net assets of less than $6 million. Those thresholds have been unchanged for almost 20 years. The maximum net asset value test was first introduced in 1999, with the Howard government's discount. Anthony Albanese I move: That the amendments be agreed to. Our Labor government is delivering real change to make a real difference—real change built on Australian values: fairness, aspiration and opportunity for all. A $250 tax cut for working Australians, a $1,000 instant tax deduction and a fair crack for first home buyers—these reforms are for young Australians who have been locked out of the housing market for too long, but they're also for their parents and grandparents who want to see the next generation have the opportunity and security of a roof over their head. These reforms are also about rebalancing our tax system and better aligning income from work compared to income derived from assets. Overwhelmingly, most Australians have nothing to sell but their time and nothing to give but their hard work. That is how most Australians earn their income. They work their guts out every day to provide for their families and put food on the table, and for too long the economy has not been working for them. We want an economy that works for people, not people working for an economy. Our government isn't going to sit back and let that continue. We're not going to kick the can down the road. We're not going to try and explain away a broken system. We are doing something about it. We're backing aspiration, rewarding hard work and giving young people a fair crack. We are delivering real change. Young people have waited long enough for a rebalancing of that system. That is why this legislation that will give young Australians a fair crack should be supported by this parliament, so that young Australians can get access to their own home. Moved the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, proposing worker tax relief, a $1,000 instant deduction, first-home ownership measures, indexed capital gains taxation and limits on negative gearing for existing residential properties.

Moved that two tax reform bills be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics, arguing that rushed legislation required scrutiny of effects on housing, young people, small businesses, startups, productivity and fairness.

Moved to vary sitting arrangements on 2 and 3 June 2026 to prioritise taxation bills, then moved that debate on two tax reform bills not conclude until every government member had spoken; the motions were agreed to with an absolute majority.
Moved to allow two taxation bills to be debated together and moved that the question be put; the question on the motion was then before the House.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for an advisory report by 30 December 2026, then moved that government business order No. 2 be called on immediately.

Supported tax reform bills that would replace the capital gains tax concession with cost-base indexation from 1 July 2027, limit negative gearing on later-purchased rental properties to new homes, introduce a $250 working Australian tax offset and create a $1,000 instant deduction, arguing the changes would improve fairness and housing affordability.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so debate on the tax reform bills would not conclude until every government member had spoken, then moved that the question be put and later that debate be adjourned, while arguing members should be accountable for the budget's measures.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for consideration and an advisory report by 30 December 2026.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so specified amendments and remaining stages of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 could be grouped, debated briefly, and put to immediate questions, then moved that the question be put.

Argued that the tax reform bills contain welcome measures on property concessions but require fuller scrutiny, and foreshadowed amendments to split the bill, clarify startup and employee equity protections, limit ministerial powers, protect grandfathered concessions, exempt testamentary trusts, add income protections and reinvest revenue in social and affordable housing; other contributions disputed the bills' effects and supported or opposed them.

Moved procedural motions setting the Senate's hours, business sequence and voting limits for 23 to 29 June 2026, including expedited consideration of tax, appropriation, secrecy, workplace-relations and other bills; then argued that the agreed tax reforms would damage home saving, business growth and aspiration, promising their repeal under a future coalition government.

Opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing they would reduce investment, business formation and housing opportunities, and criticised proposed exemptions that would require bureaucrats to determine which businesses are innovative.

Moved opposition amendments to remove the capital gains tax and negative gearing schedules from the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing the package would raise taxes, increase compliance costs and harm housing, investment and businesses; the government said those measures funded tax offsets and rebalanced taxation, before the committee reported progress.

Reported and explained government amendments to the tax reform bills, including raising the active-asset concession threshold from $2 million to $10 million, exempting specified income-support recipients from the minimum capital-gains tax, and removing or narrowing ministerial powers; questions and answers addressed projected revenue, compliance costs and classic-car treatment.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026
This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed in Australia.
The package would replace the current 50% capital gains tax discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with a system that adjusts the cost base for inflation, so only real gains are taxed.

It would also introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains from 1 July 2027, with an exemption for some income support recipients, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Replace the 50% capital gains tax discount with cost base indexation for individuals, trusts and partnerships.
Introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.
Apply the new rules prospectively from 1 July 2027, including to gains on pre-CGT assets, while retaining the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Individuals, trusts and partnerships that make capital gains.

Moved the second reading of the Superannuation (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Imposition Bill 2026, which operates with related legislation to support the proposed superannuation reforms, and commended it to the House.

Argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Bill 2026 imposed an unmandated tax and threatened retirement security, while the government said it would better target concessions, strengthen the LISTO and support low-income workers.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so two superannuation bills could be debated in cognate, with variations limited to motions moved by a Minister; a motion to put the question was subsequently moved.

Asked about making superannuation fairer and more sustainable; the Treasurer said the Superannuation (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Imposition Bill 2026 was likely to pass without amendment, increasing support for low-income members while making concessions for larger balances more sustainable.

Opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Bill 2026 and related bill, arguing they imposed a new superannuation tax, weakened certainty and reflected excessive government spending. Later speakers supported the bills, highlighting LISTO changes that would benefit 1.3 million Australians, around 60 per cent of them women.

Treasury Laws Amendment (Fuel Excise Relief) Bill 2026

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Fuel Excise Relief) Bill 2026 be read a second time, proposing temporary reductions to fuel excise and the heavy vehicle road user charge in response to global conflict, disrupted supply chains and rising prices. The bill would halve fuel excise, reduce the road user charge to zero temporarily, defer its scheduled six per cent increase and provide ministerial flexibility for further changes; debate was interrupted.
Moved and commended Appropriation (Fuel Security Response) Bill (No. 2) 2025-2026 to the House, with debate adjourned and its resumption ordered for a later hour that day.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Bill 2026

Moved the second reading of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Bill 2026, proposing higher LISTO support for eligible low-income workers and reduced concessional tax treatment for future earnings on superannuation balances above $3 million, with further changes applying above $10 million.

Moved that the Superannuation Guarantee Charge Amendment Bill 2025 be read a second time, explaining that it would impose the charge for each day wages are paid when contributions are short, alongside payday super reforms.
